summary: Reserves the Extended Master Session Key (EMSK) from EAP for the sole purpose of deriving root keys. Root keys are master keys that can be used for several purposes identified by usage definitions. The memo also specifies a way to avoid conflicts between root keys by deriving them in a way tied to their intended use.

plainLanguage.summary: After you log in to a network, the equipment needs a secret key. This RFC says how to turn that one secret into a separate key for each service that needs one, in a way that keeps the services independent of each other.

questions: what is the emsk in eap
subtitle: Turning the master key from a network login into separate keys for separate uses.

tldr.problem: A network login produces a master key, and several different services would like to use it, which would tie their security to each other and to the network layer.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reserves the Extended Master Session Key for one job only: deriving root keys, each labelled with the use it is for, so that no key can be derived from another.
tldr.outcome: Each service gets its own root key, and a compromise of one service's key does not give an attacker the keys of the others or the master key itself.

today: RFC 5295 is a Proposed Standard. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it reserves the Extended Master Session Key of RFC 3748 for the single purpose of deriving root keys.

sections.title: What the Document Sets Out to Do
sections.content:
The document deals with keys generated by the authenticated key exchange mechanisms of the EAP framework. EAP defines two kinds of keying material: a Master Session Key and an Extended Master Session Key. The EAP specification implicitly assumes that the Master Session Key will be used for a single purpose at a single device, but it reserves the Extended Master Session Key for future use. This document defines the Extended Master Session Key to be used solely for deriving root keys, using the key derivation it specifies.

The root keys are meant for specific purposes, which the document calls usages. A special class of usage is the Domain-Specific Root Keys, which are made available to and used within specific key management domains. The document also gives guidelines for creating usage definitions for the various uses of EAP key material, and for the management of the root keys. Throughout the document, the terms application and usage refer to a specific use case of the EAP keying material.

Several uses for keys derived from the Extended Master Session Key have been proposed, including hand-off across access points, mobile IP authentication and higher-layer application authentication. For a particular usage to make use of this specification it must specify a usage definition. The document does not define how the derived Usage-Specific Root Keys are used; it defines a framework for deriving them for different purposes so that different usages can be developed independently of one another. The goal is that the security properties of one usage have minimal or no effect on the security properties of the others.
sections.plainLanguage: Logging in to a network produces a secret. Several services may want to use it, but if they share it directly then breaking one service breaks them all. This RFC defines a way to split that one secret into a separate root key for each service.

sections.title: Why the Keys Should Not Be Used Directly
sections.content:
The Extended Master Session Key is typically established as part of network access authentication and authorization, and the keys derived from it are expected to be used in protocols related to network access, such as hand-over optimizations. The scope of those protocols is usually restricted to the endpoints of the lower layers over which EAP packets are sent.

It is therefore inappropriate for the security of a higher-layer application to rely solely on keys derived from network access authentication. Even when used together with another, independent security mechanism, the use of these keys has to be weighed against the benefit of the optimization and the need to support several solutions. Performance optimizations may not warrant the close tie-in between the layers that using EAP-based keys would require, and such optimizations may be offset by the complexity of managing the validity and use of key material. Keys generated by later EAP authentications may be beyond the knowledge and control of applications.

From an architectural point of view, applications should not make assumptions about the lower-layer technology, such as network access authentication, used on any particular hop along the path between the application endpoints. From a practical point of view, making such assumptions would complicate using the applications over lower layers that do not use EAP, and make it harder for applications and access technologies to evolve independently.

Parties using keys derived from the Extended Master Session Key also need trust relationships with the EAP endpoints and mechanisms for securely communicating the keys. For most applications it is not appropriate to assume that all current and future access networks are trusted to secure the application function; applications should implement their security mechanisms in an access-independent manner. Implementation considerations may also complicate getting the keys to an application, since in many configurations the application endpoints differ from the EAP endpoints. It is therefore not recommended to use keys derived from the Extended Master Session Key as an exclusive security mechanism when their use is not inherently and permanently tied to the lower layer where the network access authentication was performed.

One further limit: keys derived from EAP are pair-wise by nature and are not directly suitable for multicast or other group uses such as those in some routing protocols. It is possible to use them in protocols that distribute group keys to group participants, but defining those protocols is outside the scope of this document and would need a further specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The master key belongs to the network layer, and the document is careful: a higher service should not depend on it alone, because the network connection may change and the service may end up somewhere else. So the keys derived here are meant to be an ingredient in a service's security, not the whole of it.

sections.title: The Words the Document Uses
sections.content:
A usage definition is an application of cryptographic key material to provide one or more security functions, such as authentication, authorization, encryption or integrity protection, for related applications or services. The document gives guidelines for what a usage definition should contain and places no constraint on the types of use case or service that create one.

A Usage-Specific Root Key is keying material derived from the Extended Master Session Key for a particular usage definition, used to derive child keys in the way that definition sets out.

A key management domain is specified by the scope of a given root key. The scope is the collection of systems authorised to access key material derived from that key, and systems within a domain may be authorised to derive key material, to use key material, or to distribute it to other systems in the same domain. A derived key's scope is constrained to a subset of the scope of the key it came from.

A Domain-Specific Root Key is keying material derived from the Extended Master Session Key that is restricted to use in a specific key management domain, and it is used to derive child keys for a particular usage definition. Those child keys are called Domain-Specific Usage-Specific Root Keys. They are like usage-specific root keys except that their scope is restricted to the same domain as the parent key they came from.
sections.plainLanguage: The words to learn are usage, which is one particular job a key is wanted for, and domain, which is the set of systems allowed to reach the key. A domain-specific root key is the way to hand a service its own key without handing it the master key.

sections.title: Separation and Coordination
sections.content:
Because the Extended Master Session Key is used to derive keys for several use cases, the derived keys have to be cryptographically separate. Cryptographic separation means that when several keys are derived from it, given any one of them it is computationally infeasible to derive any of the others. Deriving the Extended Master Session Key from any combination of the derived keys must also be computationally infeasible. In practice this means that deriving the master key from a derived key, or deriving one child key from another, has to take as much computation as, for example, reversing a cryptographic hash function.

Separation can be achieved in several ways. One is to use a pseudo-random function on the master key and generate a key stream, taking keys of the required length from that stream. Another is to derive keys by giving the pseudo-random function different inputs. The second is preferable, because derivation of one child key from the master key is then independent of the derivation of another, so child keys can be derived in any order. That in turn means the extra input to the pseudo-random function must be different for each child key, and coordinated properly to meet the separation requirement and prevent reuse of key material between usages.

Without separation, the security of one usage depends on the security of all the other usages that derive keys from the same master key, which is undesirable. Four requirements follow. It must be computationally infeasible to compute the Extended Master Session Key from any root key derived from it. Any root key must be cryptographically separate from any other root key derived from the same master key or domain-specific root key. The derivation of usage-specific root keys must be coordinated so that two separate usages do not derive the same key, and the derivation of domain-specific root keys must be coordinated so that two separate key management domains do not derive the same key. Finally, the derivation of domain-specific root keys and usage-specific root keys must be specified so that no domain can obtain a usage-specific root key by providing a domain name identical to a usage key label.
sections.plainLanguage: Each derived key has to be useless for getting any other key, including the master key. That means the derivation has to cost as much as breaking a hash. It also means the labels have to be coordinated, so that two different services cannot end up with the same key by accident.

sections.title: How a Root Key Is Derived
sections.content:
The EMSK root key derivation function derives a usage-specific root key from the master key, a key label, optional data and an output length. The function is expected to give the same output for the same input. The basic derivation is that the root key is the derivation function applied to the master key, the key label, a NULL octet, the optional data and the length, where the vertical bar means concatenation, the NULL octet is 0x00, and the length is a 2-octet unsigned integer in network byte order.

The key labels are printable ASCII strings, unique for each usage definition, and at most 255 octets long. In general they have the form label-string at specorg, where specorg is the organisation that controls the specification of the usage definition, so that the label is globally unique. The NULL octet after the label avoids collisions when one label is a prefix of another, such as foobar and foobarExtendedV2, which is simpler than requiring an allocation policy that prevents prefixes from occurring.

The derivation function must be able to process at least 2048 opaque octets of optional data, and that data must stay constant while the function runs. A usage definition may use the EAP Session-ID in the optional data, which has the advantage that the data going into the derivation is then unique to the session that produced the keys. The function must be able to handle input keys of up to 256 bytes, and may do so by hashing long keys down to a size the underlying algorithm can consume. The length field is a 2-octet unsigned integer in network byte order giving the output key length in octets; an implementation must be able to produce at least 2048 octets of output, and root keys are recommended to be at least 64 octets long. Usage-specific root keys must be at least 64 octets in length, and a usage definition that needs a root key must specify all the inputs to the derivation other than the master key.

The specification allows different derivation functions, but in order to have coordinated derivation the same function must be used for every derivation from a given master key. If none is specified, the default one must be used. The initial authenticated key exchange may specify a favoured derivation function, for example an EAP method naming a preferred one in its own specification, and if it does, that overrides the default. Usage definitions must not concern themselves with the construction or the selection of the function; they only supply the inputs.

The default function is the PRF+ key expansion from RFC 4306, based on HMAC-SHA-256. PRF+ was chosen for its simplicity and efficiency. It produces a sequence of blocks, where the first is the pseudo-random function applied to the key and the seed with a counter octet, and each later block is the function applied to the key, the previous block, the seed and the next counter octet, continuing as needed to reach the required length. The key is the master key, and the seed is the concatenation of the key label, the NULL octet, the optional data and the length. Since PRF+ is only defined for 255 iterations, it can produce up to 8160 octets of key material.
sections.plainLanguage: Deriving a key takes four things: the master key, a label naming the use, some extra data if wanted, and the length wanted. The default function is a standard expansion based on HMAC-SHA-256, and every derivation from the same master key has to use the same function.

sections.title: Naming the Keys
sections.content:
The EAP keying framework of RFC 5247 says the master key must be named using the EAP Session-ID and a binary or textual indication. Following that requirement, the master key name is derived by applying the derivation function to the EAP Session-ID, the four ASCII letters EMSK, the NULL octet and the length, where the length is the 2-octet unsigned integer 8 in network byte order.

It is recommended that all keys derived from the master key are referred to by that name and the context of the descendant key usage, which is the default behaviour, with any exception signalled by the individual usages. Usage-specific root keys may instead be named explicitly, by applying the derivation function to the EAP Session-ID, the key label, the NULL octet, the optional data and the length, where the key label and optional data must be the same as those used in the derivation of that key and the length is again the 2-octet unsigned integer 8 in network byte order.

Explicit naming applies when there is ambiguity in referring to the keys using the master key name and the context of the usage. The usage must signal such an exception in key naming, so that both parties know the name being used.
sections.plainLanguage: Keys are given names so that the two ends can talk about them. The usual name is the session identifier combined with the master key's own name, and a usage that finds that ambiguous can ask for a name derived from its own label instead, and must then tell the other end.

sections.title: Domain-Specific Keys and What Usages Must Do
sections.content:
A particular usage-specific root key, called a Domain-Specific Root Key, is derived from the master key for a specific set of usages in a particular key management domain. Usages derive specific keys for specific services from it, and it may be distributed to a domain so that keys can be derived inside that domain. The domain-specific root key is a usage-specific root key with the key label dsrk@ietf.org and optional data holding the domain label, which must be an ASCII string naming the key management domain the key is for. It must be at least 64 octets long.

The Domain-Specific Usage-Specific Root Keys are derived from the domain-specific root key with the same construction as any other usage-specific root key: the derivation function applied to the parent key, the key label, the NULL octet, the optional data and the length, with labels at most 255 octets and optional data of at least 2048 octets. Usages that use the domain-specific root key must define how the peer learns the domain label to use in a given derivation, and a multi-domain usage must define how both the domain-specific root keys and the specific keys are transported to the different domains. The master key name should be sent along with the domain-specific root key, unless a name of its own is expected, and the usage must signal that exception too.

Where it is appropriate for only one domain to be authorised to perform a function, the usage should not be defined as multi-domain. Where only certain domains are authorised for a multi-domain usage, the domains without full authorisation should not receive the domain-specific root key and should receive only the specific keys for the usages they are authorised for.

A usage definition has to meet a list of requirements. It must say whether it is a domain-enabled usage. It must not use the master key in any way other than deriving root keys with the derivation this document specifies, and must not use the master key directly. It should not require the master key to be cached, and it is recommended that the root key derived for it is used to derive child keys instead. It must define distinct key labels and optional data, and it must define the length of its root keys, recommended to be at least as long as the master key, which is itself at least 64 octets. It must define how it uses its root keys.

The guidelines for managing the root keys add that a root key should only be used for deriving child keys, that the usage must specify how and when that derivation happens, and that enough entropy should be introduced to support the number of keys derived. The lifetime of a root key should not be longer than that of the master key, so that when the master key expires the root keys derived from it are removed from use, and a usage should begin to use the new root keys from a later EAP transaction as soon as possible. The master key never leaves the EAP peer and server, though some root keys are provided to other entities, and when they are, the master key name and the lifetime must be transported with them.

The EAP system itself has its own requirements: the master key must not be used for any purpose other than this derivation, must be secret and not known to anyone observing the exchange, must be kept inside a protected location where only root keys derived by this specification may be exported, and must be unique for each EAP session. The EAP method must provide an identifier for the transaction that produced the key, and the system must define which usage definitions are used and how they are invoked. The Master Session Key may be used as before for backward compatibility, but new usage definitions following this specification must not use it, and implementations must prevent two usages from using it, because then the separation would not be achieved.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain gets its own root key, which is then used to make the keys that domain's services need. A domain that is only partly trusted gets only the keys it is allowed, not the parent key. Each usage has to say what it wants, how long its keys last, and that it will not use the master key for anything else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The effective strength of the derived keys is never greater than the strength of the master key, or of a master key internal to the EAP mechanism. The intent of the derivation function is to produce keys that are cryptographically separate, so that the compromise of one usage-specific root key does not compromise the others or the master key, and it is believed that the chosen function provides that separation.

An implementation of an EAP framework should keep the master key internally as close to where it is derived as possible and only offer an interface for obtaining root keys. It may also restrict which callers have access to which keys. A usage definition must not assume that any entity outside the EAP server or peer has access to the master key, and in particular must not assume that a lower layer has access to it.

Where root keys have to be distributed from where they are generated, they are secret keys, so they must be transported with their integrity and confidentiality maintained, between authenticated and authorised parties. The context of the key usage has to travel with the key, including information identifying it and constraints on its use such as its lifetime. The document does not define a key transport mechanism; that is left to usage definitions and the systems using them.

The key lifetime depends on how the key is generated and used, and the usage definition must decide how long it is valid for. Lifetime or strength information from the authenticated key exchange should be used when it is available, and lifetimes should be coordinated across the system where possible. A lifetime shorter than the system lifetime may leave keys invalid with no convenient way to refresh them, and a longer one may mean the key is used beyond its recommended lifetime.

On entropy, the number of root keys derived from the master key is expected to be low, and no randomness has to be introduced into the master-key-to-root-key derivation beyond the root key labels. If many keys are to be derived from a root key, it is therefore important that the derivation of child keys introduce fresh random numbers for each key.
sections.plainLanguage: The derived keys can never be stronger than the master key they came from, and they are meant to be independent of one another. Keys that leave the machine have to travel securely with their name and lifetime attached, and each usage decides how long its keys are good for.

viz.caption: THE DERIVATION FORMULAS, VERBATIM FROM RFC 5295

data.title: Derivations
data.code:
USRK    = KDF(EMSK,  key label | "\0" | optional data | length)
DSUSRK  = KDF(DSRK,  key label | "\0" | optional data | length)
EMSKname = KDF(EAP Session-ID, "EMSK" | "\0" | length)

viz.caption: THE INPUTS OF A ROOT KEY DERIVATION

items.title: EMSK
items.text: The key the root key is derived from. It never leaves the EAP peer and server.

items.title: Key label
items.text: A printable ASCII string of at most 255 octets, of the form label-string at specorg.

items.title: Optional data
items.text: At least 2048 opaque octets, constant during the derivation. It may hold the EAP Session-ID.

items.title: Length
items.text: Two octets in network byte order giving the length of the output key in octets.

viz.caption: THE FOUR RULES ON SEPARATION AND COORDINATION

cells: The EMSK cannot be computed from any root key
Working back to the master key
Any two root keys from the same EMSK or DSRK are separate
One usage being compromised through another
Two usages deriving the same key
Two domains deriving the same key
